subtopic: SMALL AND MEDIUM BUSINESS WEEK 1987 TRIBUTE TO CANADIAN ENTREPRENEURS-IMPORTANCE OF ENTREPRENEURSHIP

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development); Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: SMALL AND MEDIUM BUSINESS WEEK 1987 TRIBUTE TO CANADIAN ENTREPRENEURS-IMPORTANCE OF ENTREPRENEURSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this is the first day of Small Business Week 1987, a very important event in Canada.
Small Business Week gives us an opportunity to pay tribute to Canadian entrepreneurs. After all, the entrepreneur provides the spark that starts small businesses. An entrepreneur is someone who takes risks, works, worries and finally creates something that did not exist before.
The theme of Small Business Week 1987, the creative power of entrepreneurship, is therefore very apt.

The facts speak eloquently of the importance of small business to our national economy. There are more than three quarters of a million small businesses in Canada. Some
155,000	new ones are started each year. They employ 40 per cent of the workers and are creating 67 per cent of all the new jobs our economy produces, 100 per cent in some regions of the country. Local entrepreneurs, therefore, form the cornerstones of the Government's regional development policies.
Close to a third of all small businesses are owned by women and small businesses provide well over three million jobs for yotng men and women in Canada, an impressive 50 per cent more than big businesses provide. Small businesses are increasingly the mainstay of developed economies world-wide. They are turning more and more to small enterprise, to information-based, high technology, service-oriented activities, and away from megaprojects.

I think the Government, educational institutions and the private sector have a duty to encourage and support entrepreneurship.
Governments must first of all do everything they can to create an environment that is conducive to the development of entrepreneurship. Our Government has always tried to provide an economic climate in which people with ideas would be encouraged and supported.
The results are conclusive. For the first time in eight years, the prime rate, the inflation rate and the unemployment rate are all below the 10 per cent line. Interestingly, for the entrepreneur these lower rates mean an annual savings of $1,000 on every $33,000 of debt.
All observers have acknowledged our budgets were favourable to small businesses.
We have also implemented a plan to reduce the paper burden, and we have started to deal with regulatory and tax reform. And we are now liberalizing our trade relations with United States.

Canada's small business community welcomes freer trade. A survey of 22,528 business people conducted by the CFIB in 1986 proved that those who foresaw positive results and new opportunities from freer trade outnumbered those who saw a negative impact by nearly three to one. Now that we have a deal, Canada's entrepreneurs can and will seize the new opportunities of this historic free trade agreement and they will have far greater access to the largest, richest and closest market in the world.
Small business persons in this country are not afraid to compete because they have confidence in their abilities and so does the Government. Our efforts cannot stop there. We must all. Government, education and the private sector, turn our efforts toward stimulating new entrepreneurship across our country.

Increasingly, our education system will have to include entrepreneurship as a career choice for students. One is not born an entrepreneur, one becomes one. We can and we must teach entrepreneurship and consider it on the same level as medicine, law or engineering.
We must make Canadians understand the importance of entrepreneurship. We must encourage Canadians, especially

our young people, to become entrepreneurs, and we should support them.

I want to thank the organizers of Small Business Week 1987, the Chamber of Commerce of Canada and the Federal Business Development Bank, to commend them for their efforts and to wish them the utmost success. Let us hope that Small Business Week will contribute not only to a greater understanding and appreciation of Canada's entrepreneurs but, most importantly, to the development of new entrepreneurs upon whom so much of our future depends.

I call on all Members of this Flouse and on Canadians from coast to coast to join me in paying tribute to Canadian entrepreneurs and promoting entrepreneurship during Small Business Week 1987.

subtopic: SMALL AND MEDIUM BUSINESS WEEK 1987 TRIBUTE TO CANADIAN ENTREPRENEURS-IMPORTANCE OF ENTREPRENEURSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to thank the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism), who gave us prior notice of his statement. Speaking on behalf of the Official Opposition and the Liberal Party of Canada, I too wish to pay tribute to the men and women who, with perseverance, creativity and courage, have started many small businesses, some of which have later become full scale enterprises. These men and women, as the Minister pointed out, are responsible for 70 per cent of the jobs in this country. During the recession in the first part of this decade, when big companies were closing and jobs were being lost, small businesses were still creating jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit 1 am somewhat disappointed today. I expected the Minister would take advantage of this opportunity to announce new programs that would help develop small businesses and promote their growth, and thus create even more jobs.
Looking at the statistics, if every small business could create one more job, we would have about 800,000 new jobs, which would reduce unemployment considerably in this country. However, the Minister just went on mouthing the usual phrases, that it was a good thing this sector creates so many jobs and that there was so much development in this sector. Where are the programs?
Of course, the Minister referred to reduced tax rates. Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to take this opportunity to remind the Minister that in its tax reform, the Government reduced general corporate taxes from 36 to 28 per cent-a total of 8 per cent, and reduced the manufacturing tax for large companies from 30 per cent to 23 per cent-another 7 per cent. However, the tax rate for small businesses was reduced from 15 to 12 per cent, a meager 3 per cent. In fact, he increased the tax rate for small manufacturers by 2 per cent, raising the tax from the present 10 per cent to 12 per cent, effective next year if the tax reform becomes effective on January 1, 1988, as promised by the Minister of Finance.
Mr. Speaker, that is what this Governement has done for small business. Today, the Government is paying tribute to this sector, to all these men and women who have contributed so much to the economic development of our country, and at the same time, the Government has proposed measures to discourage this development.
The tax reform also includes the $500,000 capital gains reduction. We agree with the principle, but on closer inspection, it is just window dressing. It does not really do anything for small businesses because, as we all know, 50 per cent of small businesses are not incorporated, and the measure only applies to the sale of shares. Among the other 50 per cent who are incorporated, Mr. Speaker, the majority do not sell their shares, only their assets. So until this measure also applies to the assets of small businesses, our small Canadian entrepreneurs will not be able to take advantage of this exemption.
In the past few months, the Minister has been congratulating himself on having created an advisory committee to cut paper burden. I may remind him that in 1983, the Liberal Government set up a similar advisory committee to deal with all these problems that were impeding the economic development of small businesses. In the fall of 1984, when the Conservative Government came to power, the advisory committee, which included representatives from various small business groups, was abolished outright, and it was not until 1986 that the Government acknowledged its mistake and reinstated the advisory council. What the Conservative Government has done for small businesses in the last three years boils down to a great big zero.
I am very disappointed, Mr. Speaker, because the Minister could have taken this opportunity to unveil really new programs.
I should like to recall that in 1985 the former Minister of State (Small Businesses) had undertaken to consult all Canadians precisely to learn what small businesses are all about. The Government spent a small fortune, Mr. Speaker, but we never did get the report because apparently it was printed but not distributed mainly because it did not have anything new to say. After three years I would have hoped that since the new Minister has held this portfolio for a year now, I would have hoped . . .
When I learned Friday that the Minister would be making a statement in the House today to mark the opening of Small Business Week 1 was hoping he would announce new programs, but no such luck. All we got are still more pious wishes, but small business has no use for pious wishes, it wants action, it wants to create jobs and help the community. But the Government has failed to respond, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on behalf of my Party. Small- and medium-sized businesses are a major component of our society. They create a lot more jobs than the big multinationals ever do, and the small business international fund will remain


the major source of new jobs for Canadian men and women. Small businesses now employ 42 per cent of Canada's paid labour. As emphasized recently by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, small businesses with fewer than 19 employees accounted for 86 per cent of employment between 1975 and 1982, while companies with more than 100 employees reported a 6 per cent employment drop.
Mr. Speaker, that is how important small-and medium-sized businesses are here in Canada.
Recently we in the NDP organized a task force concerning the creation of jobs. One important area we identified was the need to do more for small business. We recommended the following nine points and 1 want to put them very quickly on the record.
First, ensure that banks provide more loans to small businesses at rates given to big businesses.
Second, establish a more aggressive "buy Canadian" program which includes government contracts and is targeted to small business and community enterprises. That of course becomes more difficult with the free trade agreement if it indeed goes through.
Third, provide risk and venture capital for small businesses.
Fourth, provide greater opportunities for women to establish small businesses, including a commitment by the banks to treat women in an equal manner. Recently it has been women more than men who have been successful in establishing small businesses.
Fifth, identify areas in which small businesses could expand to meet consumer demand now covered by imports. Again I have concerns about this area when it comes to free trade.
Sixth, provide small businesses with relevant financial, marketing and management assistance through federal "one-stop shopping centres" to be organized in conjunction with local business communities.
Seventh, reform the Federal Business Development Bank to refocus its activities on small businesses, especially those most in need.
Eighth, direct the Canada Patent Development Corporation to work with small business to help them patent new innovations and market those patents world-wide.
Ninth, change the tax system to make severance pay tax exempt and allow the tax-free use of RRSPs to start up new small businesses.
Those are some of the recommendations our Party made as a result of its special task force on jobs two years ago.

The committee is greatly impressed with the dedication, hard work, and competence of public servants in general who come before us insofar as their commitment to delivering the programs of their departments. Mr. Speaker, I recall the secret Government free trade communication strategy document that was leaked over two years ago. It said:
The strategy should rely less on educating the general public than on getting across the message that the trade initiative is a good idea. In other words a selling job.


From the outset of these negotiations the Government of Canada has deliberately kept Canadians in the dark, deliberately kept the facts from Parliament, and deliberately refused to give us the parameters of the authority of the negotiating team. That has been the Government's strategy from the beginning and continues to be its strategy. It is a cynical, manipulative and misleading tactic. There is one thing wrong with it; Canadians are not stupid, Canadians will not be fooled, and Canadians will not buy this trade deal.
Some Flon. Members: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada went into this trade negotiation under three naive assumptions. The first was that obtaining an agreement with the United States would somehow magically exempt Canada from protectionist sentiment in the United States, particularly in the U.S. Congress. That was naive from the outset.
Leading members of the Congress, the U.S. Senate, and the House of Representatives told us publicly and privately on trips to Ottawa that there was no way Canada would gain an exemption from U.S. trade remedy law as set forth in the 1974 trade law of the United States or, indeed, in the Omnibus Bill currently before the Senate and House of Representatives. We were warned that there was no way that would happen. Yet the Government laboured under the naive assumption that a signed agreement would somehow exempt us from that.
We can see from the agreement that we have not been exempted. American trade law and practice, present and future, will continue to apply to Canadian exports. We have not gained secure access to the American market.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The second naive assumption was that we could get a quick fix. Instead of dealing multilaterally and internationally through the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, as we did so successfully during the Kennedy Round and the Tokyo Round, the Government tried to get a quick fix to our trade problems by dealing bilaterally and directly with the United States. Going head-to-head, face-to-face, one-on-one with the strongest economic power in the world, which is ten times stronger than we are, when our Government wanted to deal politically more than their Congress wanted to, we were bound to get a lousy deal. That is what happened. We got a lousy deal.
Of course, the third naive assumption was that the United States really wanted free trade with Canada. The United States does not want free trade. It is clear now that they have always wanted fair trade according to their definition as it is set out in the 1974 congressional law and as it is set out in the Omnibus bill.
Supply
Fair trade means trade in reciprocal terms, trade on their terms. They used the level playing field but it is their playing field, with their rules, their linesmen, their goalposts, their ball and their uniforms. That is what the United States always wanted in a trade agreement and that is what they have received in this particular deal.
The timing could not be worse for Canada. The United States and the Reagan administration has been pulling world demand into their market. The American market has kept the world economy going, but it became evident over the last number of months that a trade deficit of the proportions being run by the United States and the extent of the budgetary deficit, financed by Japan and Germany, could not continue forever and that the United States could no longer fuel world demand.
It has become evident that it will have to convert itself into a neutral and surplus position, which will be at the expense of every other country in the world. There is no way that the United States Congress and the United States administration, particularly in light of last week's events on the stock market, can afford not to take control of their trading position. Therefore, nothing could be worse in terms of timing and nothing will reflect congressional sentiment more acutely.

But the Government was naive. They presumed that by simply sitting down with the United States and negotiating a trade deal we would, as if by magic, be exempted from the American protectionist legislation and guaranteed free access to the U.S. market. But there is no magic in international trade. There is no miracle and no ready-made solution either, and it is clear that the results are not there for Canada.
To achieve his objectives, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) needed to convince the Americans of two things: first, to write down specifically in the agreement that Canada would no longer be subjected to any American protectionist legislation and, second, to set in place a binding dispute settlement mechanism to settle any dispute between the two countries. These conditions were essential. Well, the Mulroney Accord does not meet either of these conditions. The Accord does not guarantee free access to the American market. It does not protect us from protectionist legislation.

What does the dispute mechanism say? It is still to be determined whether it is constitutional under American law. The dispute mechanism is only a review panel. It applies American law and American practice to our exports. Nothing is changed. Its only leverage under the American administrative tribunal is to analyse whether those tribunals have applied correctly American law and American rules according to their practice. It does not change the law to which Canada is subject regarding the American market. It changes a judge and prolongs the process.


Supply
When we consider the softwood lumber case, it prolongs the process probably by another litigious year. That softwood lumber case would have been decided under the same law and rules. Furthermore, that 15 per cent tax for our softwood lumber going into the American market has been grandfathered and made part of the treaty.
In March, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) said that the objective of any trade agreement would be the elimination of countervail in both countries. In April, the Prime Minister said that the U.S. trade remedy law cannot apply to Canada. That seemed quite clear and sensible. The only reason to attempt to seek an agreement would be to get an exemption from U.S. trade law. The Minister for International Trade and the Prime Minister understood it then, but last week the chief negotiator for Canada, Simon Reisman, said that it is "just plain dumb" to think "that this agreement should provide us with an exemption from American trade remedy laws, is just the silliest proposition I have ever heard."
That flies right in the face of the Prime Minister's remarks, and right in the face of the instructions obviously given to him by the Minister for International Trade when she went public on that very important issue. She was right then and the Prime Minister was right then; without an exemption of U.S. trade law an agreement is not worth the paper it is written on. That is the reason we oppose it.
Why does the Prime Minister continue to tell us that that is what he achieved in this agreement, when his chief negotiator says that it is just not so. In his revised summary of the agreement, Mr. Yeutter says:
The U.S. countervailing duty and anti-dumping laws-defined as U.S. statutes, legislative history, regulations, administrative practice, and court decisions-will remain intact and unchanged. Hence, U.S. petitioners will retain all their rights under existing U.S. law, just as Canadian industries will keep their rights under Canadian law.
We are back to where we started. We do not have that secure access to the American market that the Prime Minister promised and which he himself recognized as essential for any deal.
Let us also get rid of some of the philosophical baggage. This is not a free trade arrangement. This is a selective trade arrangement and Members of Parliament and Canadians are entitled to look at this deal on its merits. Some industries are in; some industries are out. The British Columbia wine industry and the Ontario wine industry are in; the breweries are somehow out. Apparently communications are out while textiles are in.

Flow does one explain that to textile workers who are vulnerable, while brewery workers are protected? How does one explain that to the footwear and clothing industry workers who are vulnerable, while the television community is protected? How does one explain that to the electronic industry workers in Quebec and Ontario who are vulnerable, while the Dow, Labatt, and Molson brewery workers are protected? We
must therefore scrutinize the agreement and realize that we have gained very little while giving up a lot.

We did not get that secure access to the American market. Yet we have opened our investment to the Americans, opened our culture, opened our capital markets, and our agriculture. We changed the Auto Pact and have become a storehouse in a continental energy policy.
We have lost control over investment because the thresholds have risen dramatically. I said in the House some three weeks ago that takeovers will be unlimited and it will be open season for the Americans.
Our service sectors, particularly our financial markets, are now open and we will have lost control over those markets as an element in determining Canadian economic policy.
No one could have predicted that a continental energy policy would be in this agreement. There was never any sense that we were not only negotiating a trade agreement but that we were selling the resource base of this country or, to put it in more realistic terms, giving away the resource base of this country.
Since Confederation we have always resisted American pressure by building a country east and west and north. We built a railway, we built an airline, we built a broadcasting system and we built a pipeline. We moved against those natural forces that would have brought us into the American orbit. Yet the Government, in one fell swoop, and with one signature, has thrown that away. Our oil, gas and coal are now directed into a continental resource basket and we have become a resource storehouse for the United States. We no longer control our own energy policy.
How many times were we told that our cultural industries were not on the table? Yet Clayton Yeutter, the U.S. Trade Representative, told us in his summary: "Canada has agreed that cultural measures it takes will not impair the benefits the U.S. would otherwise expect from the provisions of the agreement". Just to make sure that we got the point, he revised his summary and stated:
The U.S. retains the right to redress any adverse commercial effects of any
future cultural measures enacted by Canada.
The Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) is here and she may want to speak about that.
The warning is clear. If a future government of Canada decides to support Canadian art and culture in a way that the Americans consider has an adverse commercial effect on them, then they will retaliate. That is the interpretation the U.S. puts on this agreement. So much for culture not being included.
How many times did the Prime Minister and his Ministers tell us that agriculture was not on the table? We do not have much time to go into that this morning but I will say that the


whole supply management structure of this country is vulnerable because the seasonal import protection is lifted.

U.S. multinational corporations now will be able to make an onslaught on our markets with their fruits, vegetables, dairy products and even their TV-dinners. In that area, Canadians cannot compete with the Americans, for no fault of their own. Our season is too short. Our winters are cold here in Canada. There is no way farmers here with a three-month growing season can compete with farmers down South who enjoy a twelve-month growing season. If in order to please the Americans we sacrifice our farmers, and our fishermen, we will end up depending on them, even for the food we eat.

How many times did the Prime Minister tell us that the Auto Pact was not on the table? But there it is in the agreement, changed, perhaps gutted, and we will have to wait for the final print to see exactly how much it has been gutted. Our auto parts manufacturers, Frank Stronach in the lead, the largest in the country, and the second largest, from Belleville, Ontario, have said that as a result of this agreement they are going to move their plants into the United States. That is what they said.
How many times did the Prime Minister tell us that the agreement would create thousands and thousands of jobs? Yet after the deal was signed, on his first pronouncement, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) announced that up to 500,000 jobs could be lost.
I might say, and not in any way peripherally, that two-thirds of the jobs which are vulnerable under this trade agreement with the United States are filled by women, jobs in the textile industry and in the service industries, and I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, we will have more to say on that particular subject as this debate proceeds.
The whole history of these negotiations before, during and now that we see the principles of agreement, has been that the Government has thrown away our cards, our sovereignty and the tools we need for political and economic independence. Even before the Government sat down at the bargaining table the Foreign Investment Review Act had been changed and the National Energy Program had been scuttled. During the course of the negotiations it was book publishing, then during the course of the negotiations, it was our drug manufacturing situation; then potash; and then softwood lumber. Now we have added to that list the auto pact, agriculture, energy, financial institutions, the wine industry, textiles, and capital markets. It amounts to the most massive sell-out in Canadian history, and I and my Party will never accept it. Neither, we believe, will the vast majority of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's trade agreement will mean deep changes for this country. Never was that option discussed during the last election campaign. The Prime
Supply
Minister has no mandate to trade away our sovereignty. I will fight that agreement. I will fight it to the point of running the next election on it. You have my word for it. That is a promise.
And if Canadians give us their confidence, if they make us their government, never will I feel bound politically by that agreement signed by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade, under orders from this Prime Minister. We never signed that Agreement. We will not live with it.

We did not negotiate the deal, we are not bound by the deal, we will not live with this deal, and if the deal and the final contract reflects the principles and the general terms of agreement we have seen, we are going to tear the deal up.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I happen to believe that Canadians can compete with anyone, including the Americans. I believe we can compete without sacrificing our sovereignty and political independence. The exclusive focus on the American market, our most vital market and one that is absolutely essential for us, has cost us markets in the Pacific Rim and markets in Europe, and I went into those figures the last time I had the honour to stand in the House on this issue.
We need a global multilateral approach. We have always had greater leverage with the United States using the international negotiations to cut the deals we have cut from the Tokyo Round to the Kennedy Round. Using those international negotiations we have achieved our present situation where 85 per cent of everything we move across the border already goes in free of duty. The mistake the Government made was to go head-to-head with the United States for political purposes when it was drooling for a deal, sacrificing our principles, our citizens, our businesses and control over our economy.
It comes down to a simple question. Do we have faith enough in our fellow citizens and in ourselves to compete with the world and win? Or do we need an exclusive deal with the United States and hope it will do it for us? That is a prospect, by the way, which looks less and less likely as the United States finally has to come to terms with its own trade deficit and its own economy as a result of the cataclysm of last week. Are we willing to yield to the Americans that style of control over our economic and political decision-making process? I do not believe we are and I do not believe we should.
I have faith in this country. I have faith in Canadians and I have faith that we are mature enough, talented enough, confident enough and tough enough to make our own choices in our own way for our own future.

speechtext:
I would like to ask the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition a question. The entire lumber industry has taken a position in favour of this agreement. It has said that had a dispute settling mechanism been in place, as proposed in the agreement, it would have been able to deal successfully with the softwood lumber issue and the shakes and shingles issue would not have surfaced as it has. We also look today at the potash industry in Saskatchewan. But let us stick to British Columbia because the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition represents a riding in British Columbia.
How about the Bentleys, the Bensons, the Clarkes and all the people in these industries who are advocating that we support this initiative. How can the Right Hon. I will willingly speak at this point to add to what has been said on behalf of my Party.
The people of Canada at no point since the Second World War have had the occasion to witness such an incredible sellout of Canadian interests as we have seen presented by the Government of Canada in the last two weeks to the people of Canada on this subject.
I wish to begin my comments with a quote from an early speech made in the House by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) after he formed the Government. The Prime Minister stated on November 7, 1984, and I quote:


Supply
-we have only been in power for two months, but I can tell you this: Give

This was stated by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons two months into office.
I have a quote from Ambassador Yeutter, the principal person involved in these negotiations from the American side. Ambassador Yeutter stated last week, with the same 20-year time span in mind, "The Canadians don't understand what they have signed. In 20 years, they will be sucked into the U.S. economy".
I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that I wish the Prime Minister, when he made his comments, had told the people then that he had this 20-year scenario in mind. I can tell the Prime Minister that the New Democratic Party and Canadians from coast to coast do not accept the premise of Mr. Yeutter's conclusion. They do not accept these trade talks. They do not accept the Tory view of Canada that the only way of becoming a confident Canadian is to become an American. We believe that confident Canadians will stand up in this historic debate to fight to preserve an independent Canada, whatever the Tories may wish to do.

Mr. Speaker, we have reached a turning point in our history. As an independent country, we must answer the most important question we ever had to deal with in the latter half of the twentieth century. The Trade Agreement has raised a profound concern from coast to coast about the future of our country.
As a Canadian, I firmly believe that our country's survival is at stake. Canada's survival as a sovereign and independent nation is threatened. It is as serious as that. The Mulroney Government has made all the concessions in its negotiations with the Americans: concessions in the service sector, in the agricultural sector, in the cultural sector, in the energy sector, and even concessions on investment control and regional development.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Government's negotiations is clear. Mr. Mulroney and the Conservatives want to give Canada away piecemeal. However, Mr. Mulroney may be the Prime Minister but he does not own Canada. It is our Canada, it belongs to all Canadians and he has no right to give it away.
Mr. Speaker, during the last election campaign, the Prime Minister promised more equity and honesty. He has done the exact opposite since that time, and I am referring to pensioners and tax reforms and especially the various regions in our country. We keep hearing the same thing, time and time again. The Prime Minister says one thing and does the exact opposite. Instead of honesty, openness and equity, Canadians have had broken promises, deceit and no equity. Once again, what the Prime Minister promised and what he did were two different things.
Before the election, the Prime Minister said that free trade would have an impact on our sovereignty and that he was opposed to it for that reason.

This was not only stated by the Prime Minister before the election, but by other present Ministers of the Crown who, when asked to give their opinion of the impact of this type of deal on the future of Canada, had extremely serious and negative things to say.
The present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), a former Prime Minister, stated that he opposed this type of agreement because jobs would be lost in critical sectors of the Canadian economy. He was correct in 1983 when he stated that, and it is correct today when he is the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He should be standing by that opinion today when he said it in 1983.

The words uttered by the Prime Minister before this agreement came into place in 1983, the words of the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the words of the Minister of Finance, all of whom stated that we would lose critical jobs, we would lose our sovereignty, we would become a weak sister, that such an agreement was naive and simplistic, were correct, and Canadians believe that they are correct now.

We have had occasion in the House and outside the House to call into question a number of the important details of this agreement. I wish to add to that, what I say with care, the duplicity in the whole process that the Government has involved us in. Let us look at some key elements. What the Government has been telling us here in the House is one thing, and what we find in the documents, and what the Americans themselves say are in the documents time after time turns out to be something different.
For example, the U.S. version says that the matter of Bill C-22 was in fact part of the deal. It is in the Yeutter briefing documents. It has been said publicly in statements outside of Washington in the United States. We have read it. The Americans have read it. However, once again the Government denies it. It signs one document on October 4, thinks about its implications, and then takes steps to get another document arranged for October 5 for release to the people of Canada.
We opposed that drug legislation before it was associated with this deal, and we oppose it now. We say that the Government is wrong to sell out our interests in general in this deal and in particular in the drug industry. We also say that the right to make laws in the pharmaceutical field, which would bring low prices and good benefits to the people of Canada, and sovereignty in this field should reside in Canada for Canadians, not be shifted to the United States of America.
The Government has insisted that Canadian culture is not a hostage in this deal. It has said that before the deal, and it has said it since. If we read the briefing documents prepared for Mr. Yeutter-and again we see statements made by American officials since then-another picture emerges.
In the document prepared for the American ambassador it was said categorically that the Government of Canada within a matter of weeks would give Americans in this industry exactly what they wanted. A film mogul in Hollywood yells, "pay attention to us" and the Prime Minister and the Conservative Government say, "right; how soon can we do it?". We believe that the film industry has been dominated too long in terms of its distribution by an American set of companies serving their interests. We believe that the cultural interests of Canadians should be served by making changes which are long overdue. Again we criticize the Government not only for the bad deal in general but for selling out that cultural interest in particular.
Let me refer to another example. The Prime Minister says that we now have secure access to the American market-he has said this since the deal-and that we have protection from unfair and punitive U.S. action with the so-called wonderful dispute settlement mechanism which has been put in place.
While the Government is saying that, what do the Americans say? They are saying quite the opposite. If we look at the briefing notes prepared for Mr. Yeutter we see that he was asked to deal with the specific question and we see the
Supply
proposed answer from the highest U.S. officials. The question was this. "If these provisions had been in effect when we took our actions on shakes and shingles and on specialty steel, what would the outcome have been?" It was a hypothetical question for Mr. Yeutter to respond to after the so-called fair dispute settlement mechanism had been put in place. What was he told to reply? It was; "We believe there would be no major difference whatsoever".
The Canadian Government has boasted that it has something wonderful. The Americans who are more direct and honest have described the dispute settlement mechanism for the phoney thing that it is. I say to the Minister that it is time the Government was frank with the people of Canada. I also say to the Minister that she may think a deal is acceptable which will not change circumstances for the workers in her province in the shakes and shingles industry, but we say that it is much more important that Canadians, whether they be in shakes and shingles or tubular steel, who are affected get something fair instead of the hypocrisy which the Government is trying to pass off on them.
Not only has there been hypocrisy and misleading information given at different times about what they got in this deal, having listened to government spokespersons, I ask the House to consider how even their language has begun to shift since the deal has come down. I quote what the Prime Minister said on April 2 of this year before the deal was announced. With reference to the unfair remedy laws so frequently passed in the United States, he said, "The trade remedy laws cannot apply to Canada, period". That is what the Prime Minister said. He said that what the Government was after was getting exemption from these unfair laws. They are his words; not mine.
Now that we have the sham before us, about which the whole country knows, how is Mr. Reisman describing the same situation? The other day he was quoted in The Ottawa Citizen as saying, "That this agreement should provide us with an exemption from American trade remedy laws is just the silliest proposition I ever heard". He should have told that to the Prime Minister last April when he said that that is what he would get for us.
I have a couple of gems from the Minister herself upon which I hope she will comment when she gets to her feet. With reference to U.S. trade laws, she said the following before the deal came down: "They are not fair. If things were working smoothly, neither side would need a change. The simple fact is that the present laws are not working".

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for the question and I want to assure all Hon. Members that I did not pay him to ask me that question. In answering the question I will put a challenge to the Hon. Member. The Hon. Member asked a serious question and I want to give a serious answer. He said that unemployment in the Windsor-Oshawa belt is zero. It is not quite zero but I will accept the essential argument that unemployment, compared with many other parts of the country, is indeed low. However, the key point he makes is just false. He says this happened because of a free tfade agreement in automotive trade. With respect, that is not so. The Americans wanted completely free trade in 1965. The Government of the day said no, we cannot have free trade. The industry is overwhelmingly owned in the U.S. and they would simply sell all their cars and parts in Canada and keep the plants in Michigan or, subsequently, Georgia, California and other states. The Government then negotiated the Auto Pact which had a requirement for a certain level of investment in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: A Liberal Government.

A Liberal Government. The NDP Leader of the day, unlike what the Conservatives have been saying, was not opposed to the principle of the deal, if you read his speeches. Quite the contrary. Our Party asked that it be improved, that we take steps to provide supplementary unemployment benefits for workers displaced when the industry was rationalized. We suggested steps to be taken to increase benefits for Canadian consumers. I am pleased to say the Government responded with a special supplementary unemployment benefit program for those workers. I hope the Government learns from that if it should ever be able to go ahead with this deal, which I hope it is not.
The key point I want to make is that the Auto Pact required the Americans to make investment in Canada on a continuing basis roughly in proportion to their sales in Canada. That is not free trade but it gave employment opportunities to Canadian workers. If they did not make that investment, there was a mechanism which would come into effect and force the Americans to pay thousands of dollars in tariffs to get their cars in here. That was put in place to encourage them to make investment in Canada. It is the Conservative Government today, in this free trade pact, that wants to remove that mechanism, and we are opposed to that proposal for that reason.

Member for Oshawa and was struck by his comments regarding the duplicity of the Government with respect to what it was saying before the free trade deal became public and what it is saying now. Yet it is clear that most areas of agriculture are in the agreement. What we have been trying to pin down is the actual impact of the agreement on, for example, the two-price system for wheat.
1 asked the Minister responsible for grains and oilseeds on October 5 about what impact the removal of the licensing power of the Canadian Wheat Board over wheat, oats and barley would have. This will occur as soon as the support levels in both countries are equal. This will apparently occur for oats and barley by January 1, 1989, and for wheat perhaps in the next year or so when the current U.S. program runs out of funds. The Minister said absolutely nothing of the sort would occur.
Two days later, in the Saskatchewan Legislature, we had a comment by the provincial Premier, who also happens to be the provincial Minister of Agriculture, saying that the two-price wheat system would have to go under the free trade agreement. He went on to say that the federal Government had promised to provide compensation of $280 million.
When I asked the Minister last week if the two-price system would be destroyed she gave a kind of gobbledygook answer. Her response was that she would prefer to deal with the substance of the issue, which is that the two-price treatment of wheat will be assessed in light of the free trade agreement and decisions pertaining to it will be taken at the appropriate time.
We have the Premier of Saskatchewan saying one thing. We have the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board saying something else. We have the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) saying something else again. People just do not know-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the members of the NDP have a very simple position. They are against free trade. They do not suggest anything else. My colleague, the Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain), made an interesting point. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Did you hear my answer two minutes ago? Mr. Nystrom: Be honest, Pat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The Vice President of the NDP is Bob White. Bob White, head of the auto workers and Vice President of the NDP, is against free trade except when it involves his union members.
I would like to quote John Crispo, the professor at the University of Toronto who pointed out that Bob White's position represented "an indefensible double standard". Professor Crispo said:
Here he is representing the group of Canadian workers who have had by far the most access to the American market under the Auto Pact and he's got the gall to wander around the country and lead the opposition to free trade which would give other workers-"brothers and sisters'' he has the nerve to call them-something of the same degree of access.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: That's a big lie.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Tell the truth for once, Pat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Those are the battle lines in this debate-the future versus the past.
I would like to quote a person who is not a Conservative, a well-known Liberal, Donald Macdonald of the Canadian Alliance for Trade and Job Opportunities. He said the following which is central to this debate:
The battle will be between two different perceptions of Canada. I don't see Canada as a sort of sheltered workshop for the inefficient, the incompetent or the less than capable. 1 see our country as one with a very considerable capacity, a very considerable record of success, and with an agreement of this kind-and others to come-the ability to use these talents out in a broader world market.
That is our vision of Canada, that is the Conservative vision of Canada, and that is Canadians' vision of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The Opposition has ignored the agreement itself in its remarks today. I would like to refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the requirements and objectives which the Prime Minister set out to Canadians as the criteria on which this agreement should be judged.
First and foremost was the proposal to pursue a new trade agreement "involving the broadest possible package of mutually beneficial reductions in barriers to trade in goods and services". That is what the Prime Minister promised and that is what we delivered.
The Right Hon. Member who speaks for the Opposition says that that is virtually worthless, that it is virtually nothing. He cannot be thinking of his own constituents in Vancouver who, through the elimination of tariffs and non-tariff barriers under this agreement, will have at their disposal a market of about 35 million within a two-day truck haul.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Providing the Americans don't countervail.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The hypocrisy of the Opposition is worth noting.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: We tell the truth. There is a little difference.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
His constituents will have access to a market of 35 million within a two-day truck haul. The people from Kingston, instead of being lake-bound and forced out of the U.S. market by many tariff barriers, will now have access to it. 1 do not think that the elimination of tariffs is "virtually nothing" as the Opposition says.
Furthermore, we achieved our objective of a more predictable set of rules.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) on a point of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: With great respect, Mr. Speaker, the word is "hypocrisy" not "high-pocrisy". In either case, it is not allowed in this House.

speechtext: It's unparliamentary however you pronounce it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: I heard the word. The word was not directed at a particular Hon. Member. The Hon. Minister.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, they are obviously worried about any debate on the merits of the free trade agreement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Any time, any place. You name the network.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: We achieved our second objective of better rules and a dispute settlement mechanism. We have given ourselves five years plus two more to deal with the rules which apply to a free trade agreement. That is a major accomplishment. It has never been achieved anywhere else in the world in any kind of agreement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
We initiated these negotiations with the United States in order to enhance the largest two-way trade in the world. Canadians have always traded to prosper. We export one-third of all the goods and services we produce. We compete with the best in the world. Today three million Canadians depend on trade for their pay cheques. Like it or not, nearly 80 per cent of our exports are sold to the United States. That figure rose to that level under the previous Liberal administration.
Faced with American protectionism we had two choices; to withdraw into Canadian protectionism and isolation and watch our standard of living decline, or attempt a bold move on behalf of all Canadians.


Supply

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: A sell-out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The first was irresponsible. The second secures our future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Tories can only have two thoughts at one time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
We did not enter into free trade negotiations only to get the best possible economic deal. If that had been our goal, we would have joined the United States years ago. We are not interested only in the best economic deal. The Prime Minister conducted these negotiations with a strong sense of requirement for our political and economic selfdetermination. That is why he gave specific commitments to the Canadian people at the very outset. They were very well defined.
He promised that the agreement would maintain our political sovereignty, and it does; that it would maintain our social programs, and it does. The attempts of the Opposition to say that medicare and unemployment insurance are at risk by this agreement show how pitiful their arguments are and the depths to which they will go.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: This agreement preserves our commitment to regional development, our unique cultural identity, and our agricultural marketing systems. We have delivered on each of these commitments to Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: You have capitulated.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Far from threatening our political sovereignty, this deal will strengthen it for it is far easier for an economically strong and united country to stand in dependent and sovereign than one weak and divided.
It is interesting to reflect on a comment which Premier Bourassa made to me. He said that the single most important act of a Prime Minister in achieving nationhood was the signing of an international treaty, the Treaty of Versailles, by Robert Borden on behalf of Canada. A strong Canada is enhanced by a strong economy and market opportunities abroad.
I would like to tell the House about the good luck charm that Simon Reisman carried with him during these negotiations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Get serious.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Tell us about it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The Opposition says "tell us about it".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: A great big albatross.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I am delighted to tell them about it. His good luck charm was an 1857 Prince Edward Island penny from the time when P.E.I. was still a colony. On the penny was
inscribed the slogan: "Free Trade and Self-government". He carried that talisman with him because it rings as true today as it did then. Free trade and self-government are mutually reinforcing. A strong economy is the best bulwark for sovereign independence.
Canadians will always remain proud Canadians and with this agreement we will continue to make our own determinations on how we live, on our social policies, on medicare, unemployment insurance and pensions. Anyone who believes otherwise has not read the agreement and is irresponsible to suggest it.
Since the Opposition spends its time saying what is not in the agreement, let me tell the House what is contained in the agreement. We have agreed to phase out all tariffs between the two countries within 10 years. The only exception is a snap back for horticulture, which has an extra 10 years of protection.
We have agreed to eliminate most of the technical and health standards which have often been used as non-tariff barriers at the border. Farmers were aware that this item was keeping them out of some of their markets.
We have agreed to set rules for trade and services, an unprecedented provision in international law. Trade in services is the fastest growing sector in world trade. For the first time there will be rules between the two countries for trade in services. We have also included provisions that will allow workers to go to the United States to deal with the goods and services they sell there.
We have provided greater access to each country for investors.
We have secured markets for Canadian energy, such as British Columbia natural gas, Alberta oil, Saskatchewan uranium, and Ontario and Quebec electrical power, by enshrining this Government's energy policy.
The Opposition ignores the fact that this Government dismantled the National Energy Program. They want the freedom to put it back. We opened the borders in energy and we are saying that if the Americans do not put up barriers at the border, we will not turn off the tap. That is a fair agreement between two countries. We have secured our markets and by doing so we have secured the investment for the energy resources that Canadians need.
We have given agricultural producers new markets across the border to help cattlemen, hog producers and potato growers, among others.
We have improved the potential of the auto industry by giving Canadian parts and after-market parts makers the opportunity to compete in a much bigger market, under tougher rules of origin and by keeping in place the very safeguards to which the Member for Oshawa has alluded.


have expanded the opportunities to compete for Government purchases in the other country. We have created effective procedures and institutions for the joint administration of the agreement and the binding resolution of disputes over the application of countervail and anti-dumping actions, and have been given time to adapt those laws to emerging market conditions. We have laid the foundation for future cooperation to expand and enhance the benefits of the agreement.
Let me explain some of the implications for Canadians. There will be lower prices for consumers as tariffs come down and there is more competition. Preliminary estimates show that it could cost $8,000 less to set up a new home in Canada by the time this agreement is in place. A Canadian earning $23,000 a year will have an extra $850 a year to spend.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Where are your facts?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
They laugh! They do not like these facts. 1 will tell you where 1 get these facts. I am quoting Andrew Cohen, Director of The Consumers' Association of Canada, who says, "There is something in free trade for all consumers". Let me quote other Canadians. Jack Carr, Chairman of the University of Toronto's Economics Department predicts that, "There will be more employment, wages will be higher, there will be more benefits". We will be exporting goods and services to the United States, not jobs. David Culver, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Alcan, says: "We do not have to say to ourselves perhaps we better build the plant in the United States in order to be sure we are inside the barriers . . . We can now invest in a bigger plant in Canada, secure in the knowledge that the plant will have access to the U.S. market". Multiply that many times, and the result is more jobs in Canada, some 350,000 more jobs according to the Economic Council.
I have already indicated that Canadian professionals and service industries will have better access to the U.S. market since they will be able to travel there to work on jobs or service what they have sold. Chris Gree, President of the Canadian Association of Management Consultants, says: "I am very, very excited. With our world class expertise and our Canadian structures, I think it can have a blockbuster impact on our clients and our profession".
The Canadian auto industry will have growth potential with changes in the rules of origin and continued Auto Pact safeguards. The President of the Motor Vehicles Manufacturers Association, Norman Clark, says: "It is a reasonable basis for liberalizing trade". Larry Buganto, Chairman of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers Association calls it a step in the right direction. Dean Wilson, President of the Automotive Industries Association, describes it as: "A tremendous opportunity for the automotive after-market industry". He also said: "We know already that our workers and our plants are just as efficient as those in the United States, if not more
Supply
so, so I look forward to a healthy increase in export sales". He has the kind of confidence we are looking for.
You are indicating, Mr. Speaker, that my time has almost expired. I would ask permission of the House to continue.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I think the Hon. Minister would want a minute or two to finish her remarks.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I anticipate that I will take about as much time as the Leader of the New Democratic Party.
I want to deal with the Canadian agricultural producers because they will have greater access to the U.S. market, with less harassment. The President of the Canadian Pork Council and Chairman of the Alberta Hog Producers Marketing Board supports the agreement. He said: "I am extremely pleased, hogs being a commodity that was hard-hit by the American protectionist mood". Charles Gracey of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association says: "This is a great day for Canada". Don Jarvis, Vice-President of the Grocery Products Manufacturers says: "We will gain access to a huge market in the United States". Paul Sim of the Canadian Wheat Growers says that the agreement: "Removes the big club that is being held over our head as far as U.S. protectionism is concerned".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Let them laugh at the wheat growers of Canada.
Canadian fishermen and fish processors get far more access.
Secure markets for Canadian energy will attract investment. Bob Lamond, President of Czar Resources, said: "Investor confidence in the Canadian energy industry was destroyed by the NEP and we are now seeing it rebuilt".
In closing, I want to talk about the dispute settlement mechanism. It gives us an umpire which we did not have. It provides confidence in the knowledge that unfair applications of U.S. trade laws or Canadian trade laws will be less likely with an umpire. The Opposition says that we are playing with American baseball uniforms and using American bats. We would like to have an impartial umpire who can use a binding dispute settlement mechanism.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Oshawa that we have embarked upon an historic undertaking. It is understandable that there should be this kind of debate but I know that Canadians are world class traders and world class competitors. Whether they are the fishermen of Newfoundland, the potato growers of Prince Edward Island, the auto workers of Ontario, or workers in research and development in the west, I know they welcome the opportunity this Government has given them to show how good they can be.


Supply
It is Canadians who will make this agreement work. It is Canadians who will build a stronger and more vibrant Canada by rising to the challenge of the world competition rather than withdrawing, as the Opposition suggests, into the 19th Century. I firmly believe Canadians will choose our vision of the future. Protectionism leads to depression and liberalized trade leads to prosperity. Those are the lessons of history. That is the choice facing us all. There is no other. This Government and the people of Canada know that the Opposition offers no alternatives. We know that the free trade choice is in the best interests of us all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney). She started her speech today by saying that the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) is opposed to foreign investment, is opposed to free trade, and has never given a single alternative to free trade. I want to deal with two points; first, the Minister saying our Leader was opposed to foreign investment and, second, that he did not give any alternatives.
I want to ask the Minister why she says this, in light of the fact that when the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain) posed a question to my Leader on that very point a few moments before she rose to speak, my Leader said very clearly that we support the principles in the Auto Pact, but they are not free trade? It is a trade agreement. He said on behalf of our Party that if we could have Auto Pact type principles, sector by sector, our Party would support that kind of approach.
Our Leader also said to the Hon. Member for Mission- Port Moody that we do not oppose foreign investment if we have an arrangement where foreign investment works for Canada, where we have guarantees, where we have an accord. He made that very, very clear. Our Leader as well as other people have also spoken many times in this House about an economic strategy, an industrial strategy, particularly where it concerns foreign investment.
I want to ask the Minister of International Trade why she cannot be more honest and truthful in this House and tell the Canadian people that the Leader of our Party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa, does propose some alternatives to this free trade negotiations, that he did point out that the Auto Pact is the kind of agreement we in this Party support, and we would support that kind of agreement, sector by sector, where there are built-in guarantees for the people of Canada?
It is the time to be honest with the people of Canada. It is the time to tell the people the truth, and I want to know why the Minister of International Trade will not be forthright rather than trying to distort the position of the New Democratic Party? Please answer that question.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me go to my notes for what the Hon. Member for Oshawa said. He said it is a massive sellout.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
It is not a massive sell-out. We have dismantled the investment barriers that create the kind of vibrant economy the Hon. Member enjoys in Oshawa. He is the one who is suggesting that it should not be opened up to foreign investment.
He also said-and I hope he campaigns on this-that Americans are more honest than Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I never said they were more honest than Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Answer the question, Pat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: They are more honest than you.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: That is what he said, that Americans are more honest than Canadians. I hope he goes to an election on it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: That is not true. You are at it again.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Those are exactly the words. If he is in favour of the Auto Pact, as he has not been in the past, but as he says he is now, may I point out that he should be in favour of this agreement because it protects the Auto Pact, it makes rules of origin tougher, which benefits Canadian auto makers and workers. I have already quoted the chairman of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association. I have quoted the Automotive Industries Association. I have quoted other people in the industry. If the Hon. Member were being honest, and if he was putting the interests of his voters ahead of his own, he would be for the free trade agreement because it improves the Auto Pact.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: You didn't answer the question, Pat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney). In the trade agreement the Government of Canada seems to be saying "Me, too" to any international negotiations with regard to trade, that when it goes to the MTN, the Uruguay Round, Canada is going to backing up the United States in the elimination of agriculture subsidies.
I wonder if the Minister could tell us precisely whether the Government of Canada will be supporting the United States with regard to Section 11 of the GATT, which would remove the power of countries like Canada to have supply management systems and to have border controls? Clearly it is the position of the United States that that section of the GATT should be removed. It is crucial to Canada as to whether or not the United States succeeds in that regard. The United States has made it clear. It has published its position and proposals to the GATT. The Canadian Government has filed its position secretly. The Minister will not make them available to the farmers of Canada and to Canadian citizens generally.
Since this document says we are going to support the United States in the removal of all agriculture subsidy programs, I


wonder if the Minister can tell us if the Government will be maintaining, and fighting and opposing, the removal of Section 11 which provides for supply management systems such as we have in dairy and poultry products? Or will she knuckle under and agree to the United States' support for the removal of that section of the GATT?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously the Hon. Member was not in the House last week when 1 rose and in a Ministerial statement outlined our Canadian proposal for the MTN Round on agriculture.
I would first like to point out that the bilateral agreement we have signed with the United States is considered a major achievement by our international trading partners who feared that if the world's two largest trading partners could not sign an agreement, the MTN would fail. That was their concern. That is why our international trading partners are so pleased we have achieved this. That is why 49 countries of the Commonwealth last week in Vancouver signed the Vancouver Declaration on Trade, urging trade liberalization.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Will you please answer my question?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
It is funny, the Hon. Member takes forever to put the question but I am not allowed to answer it.
I wish to point out to the Hon. Member that in my statement in the House I pointed out that our Canadian position is that we expect to get credit, as I have said, for the fact that our programs in Canada are consistent with Article XI in the GATT. It is the programs of other countries which are inconsistent with Article 11.
